item.title: Ground stop results in side judge Don Willard serving as referee for two games on Sunday
item.description: Flight disruptions result in multiple changes to Week 10 officiating assignments.
item.content:encoded:
Friday's nationwide ground stop won't keep NFL teams from getting to their road games on Sunday. It will, however, impact the ability of officials to get to where they need to be.

The NFL has announced that officiating assignments have changed for Week 10. And the situation will result in a backup referee serving as the referee in two games on the same day.

"Due to the ongoing nationwide impact to air travel this weekend, the NFL has adjusted its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns," the NFL said in a statement. "The changes will necessitate that three backup referees — umpires Barry Anderson and Duane Heydt and side judge Don Willard [pictured] — will work as referees in the following games: Carolina-New Orleans – Duane Heydt; Jacksonville-Tennessee – Barry Anderson; Miami-Indianapolis and Pittsburgh-Cincinnati – Don Willard.

"Each of the league’s 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise."

The situation creates the likely unprecedented situation of a referee working two games in one day. Willard will handle Dolphins-Colts at 1:00 p.m. ET, and then he'll make the 109-mile trip from Indianapolis to Cincinnati for the Sunday night game.

Making the unprecedented even more unusual is the fact that Willard's usual crew (led by referee Scott Novak) wasn't scheduled to work at all this weekend.

The announcement doesn't address where the referees for those three games will be working, or what their roles will be. Shawn Smith was scheduled to be the referee for Panthers-Saints, Alex Moore was set to be the referee for Jaguars-Titans, Carl Cheffers was due to be the referee for Dolphins-Colts, and Clete Blakeman was slated to be the referee for Steelers-Bengals.

The league's statement also doesn't specify other shifts that were required as to the established crews that work together throughout the regular season.

item.title: NFL reassigns 3 officials following nationwide FAA ground stop
item.description: The ground stop order was lifted Friday night, but not before it affected games in the NFL and college football this weekend.
item.content:encoded:
The ground stop order issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday has now affected the NFL after having an impact on this weekend's college football games.

On Saturday morning, the NFL announced that several officiating assignments for Week 10 have been adjusted. Officials were reassigned to games that are within driving distance of their hometowns.

Barry Anderson and Duane Heydt, who normally serve as umpires, along with side judge Don Willard, will take on referee duties on Sunday.

Anderson will officiate the Jacksonville Jaguars-Tennessee Titans game in Tennessee; Heydt has been assigned to work the Carolina Panthers-New Orleans Saints game in New Orleans; and Willard will have double-duty first refereeing the Miami Dolphins-Indianapolis Colts game in Indianapolis at 1 p.m. ET before making the trip to Cincinnati for Sunday night's game between the Bengals and Pittsburgh Steelers at 8:20 p.m. ET.

"Each of the league's 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise," the NFL said.

The ground stop order was put in place on Friday due to a "temporary telecommunications outage" affecting air traffic control, the FAA announced.

That stop was lifted as of 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, but even with flights allowed to resume, it led to kickoff changes for some college games. Almost all of the Power Four conferences have teams that were prevented from reaching their destinations. Only the ACC has every team already ready to go. One SEC matchup — Ole Miss vs. Oklahoma — was postponed to Sunday.

"It'll be slow," Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Friday about the resumption of nationwide air travel.

It's the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11, per ABC News, which noted that this last happened in 2023. At the time, pilots were unable to access their pre-departure paperwork because the FAA NOTAM (Notice To all Air Missions) system — used to disseminate flight hazards and real-time restrictions to pilots — went down.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 NFL trade deadline is officially in the rearview mirror, and we're on to Week 10, where we'll see a couple of players in new uniforms this week — and some in their old uniforms.

Kirk Cousins rejoined the Minnesota Vikings this week via a trade with the Las Vegas Raiders. He will officially don purple this weekend against the Green Bay Packers after head coach Kevin O'Connell officially named him the team's Week 10 starter on Friday. He'll make his return to Minnesota against the very team he last faced as a Viking, when he suffered a season-ending Achilles tear. He'll look to give the offense a much-needed boost to complement Brian Flores' defense after the team's 6-2 start.

With the trade of Cousins, the Raiders officially named 2026 No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza as their starter moving forward. He'll face a tough schedule to kick off his career as a starting quarterback, with the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos on deck in Weeks 10 and 11.

item.title: Jerry Jones: "I don't think we're far away" from 18 regular-season games
item.description: As to the timeline, Jones says, "Next month? No. Next year? Maybe. [The] next year? Maybe."
item.content:encoded:
As the NFL embarks on the second half of its current 18-week regular-season schedule, it's just a matter of time before the current structure changes.

It's no secret that the NFL wants to expand the regular season from 17 to 18 games. The league is sufficiently confident about it happening that folks like Cowboys owner Jerry Jones speak of it as a given.

"I don’t think we’re far away from it," Jones said Friday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas, regarding the addition of an extra game. "I don't know how — what is far away. Next month? No. Next year? Maybe. [The] next year? Maybe. That has to be negotiated with the players.

"But it's in everybody's best interests.  You'd cut back on the preseason games. You'd have teams more develop in the first few games as the type of thing you were trying to get done in preseason. But it's in everybody's interest, and it certainly is in the players' best interest in my mind, for sure.  And having said that, I would anticipate that coming."

His comments presume the NFL Players Association will happily agree to 18 regular-season games. They likely won't. At a minimum, they'll seek major concessions in exchange for the willingness to add yet another game that counts.

The unspoken goal had been 2027. The NFL delayed picking a date for Super Bowl LXII in Atlanta in order to accommodate the possibility that the game will slide a week or two deeper into February. That would make 2028 the earliest year for expansion, as a practical matter. (Adding a game for 2027 would be possible only if the dead week between the conference championships is wiped out or if the season starts a week earlier. If an 18th game will result in a second bye, both would be required.)

Expansion by 2027 would require expedited negotiations. Expansion by 2028 would hinge on the NFL and NFLPA striking a deal within the next year or so. The union has shown no inclination, however, to engage in talks aimed at extending the current Collective Bargaining Agreement, which runs through the 2030 season.

Still, if push comes to shove, there will be 18 games. The blueprint was created in 2011. The NFL will lock the players out until the players agree to the things the owners want. Most notably, 18 regular-season games and 16 annual international games.

Beyond that, Jones's comment about the early games of the season is odd. "You'd have teams more develop in the first few games as the type of thing you were trying to get done in preseason."

He says that as if it's a good thing. It definitely is not. Already, teams struggle in September to get up to speed, given that most teams (with the exception of those assigned to the Hall of Fame Game) play only three preseason games. When the preseason reduces to two games, that's even fewer chances to prepare.

It's also fewer chances for the non-starters to get the attention of coaches and General Managers in games that don't count in the standings. It will become harder for undrafted free agents to make the 53-man rosters.

Regardless, the motivation isn't football. It's money. More inventory equals more weekends equals more broadcast windows equals more revenue.

And that likely will continue until the preseason shrinks to zero games — and the regular season expands to 20 games.

item.title: NFL predictions: 4 game picks for intriguing Seahawks vs. Raiders matchup
item.description: The Price should prove right as the Seahawks meet with a familiar face.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks are hitting the road for the first time in a month to renew their former AFC West rivalry with the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday for another must-win game. Seattle enters the game as 6.5-point favorites on the road, their second straight week being favored by FanDuel Sportsbook.

While the Seahawks are large favorites, they’ll depend on their dominant defense to get the job done yet again as their inconsistent offense is still quite injured. Seattle’s “Dark Side” defense will welcome the Raiders’ first overall pick, Fernando Mendoza, to the NFL and hope to slow Klint Kubiak’s offense, which is averaging 26.4 points per game.

Here are four bets/game picks to consider ahead of Sunday’s game.

1. Jadarian Price anytime touchdown (+190)

While Seattle’s rookie running back has battled injuries this season, it’s still hard to believe that he’s yet to find the end zone. Price has shown the most juice of any Seahawks running back and emerged as a receiving threat last week against the Cardinals.

With Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock still hampered by injuries, Price is likely to get a lot of work in the passing and running game against a struggling Raiders defense. Las Vegas’ defense has allowed large receiving days to running backs this season, with the worst coming against the Buffalo Bills when back James Cook totaled 58 yards on three catches.

While it might be hard to envision betting on the Seahawks offense after they only hung 17 on the Cardinals, a second week with Lock as the leading man should lead to a more complete game plan, allowing them to score and make a statement.

2. Maxx Crosby to record a sack (+144)

With Charles Cross out and Abe Lucas struggling this season, there’s a near guarantee that the Raiders’ star pass rusher will be active in the Seahawks backfield on Sunday. Crosby leads the Raiders with four sacks, and while he hasn’t quite been in game-wrecking self this season, he shouldn’t need to be to get home against an injured Lock.

3. Jaxon Smith-Njigba over 89.5 receiving yards (-114)

Coming off his quietest outing of the year, there’s no question that Smith-Njigba should be more involved with the Seahawks offense this week. JSN has totaled over 100 yards in all, but two of his games this season and has padded his total against poor secondaries, which should include Las Vegas’ unit.

While I already mentioned this in the Price prop, I’ll say it again: the Raiders’ defense is not good. Las Vegas secondary gives up an average of 234 passing yards per game, one of the worst marks in the league. Even though Lock is still dealing with an injury, JSN should be so open on Sunday he’ll only need half an arm to get it to him.

4. Seahawks -6.5 (-110)

Seattle head coach Mike Macdonald is undefeated against quarterbacks making their first start, and there’s no reason this game should be different. Mendoza has limited reps as a starter and is getting thrown to the wolves against a Seahawks defense that is riding high after holding an NFC West rival to just three points last week.

Lock and the Seahawks’ offense may struggle early, but there is simply too much star power for the Raiders defense to handle. Las Vegas’ defense has thrived on turnovers, so Seattle will need another turnover-free game from Lock and Price like they got last week. If the Seahawks’ offense can stay clean there’s no doubt the defense will handle Mendoza and allow the Seahawks to handle the Raiders with ease.

Final prediction: Seahawks 31, Raiders 17

Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Each week, we send out questions to the most plugged-in Kansas City Chiefs fans. You can see all of the recent survey results here.

And be sure to check out FanDuel Sportsbook, the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation.

Chiefs fans’ confidence

That’s up 22% from a week ago, when we ran the same poll.

I guess beating a bad team does that for you. Nothing instills confidence in a team like your team bullying a lesser opponent and stealing their lunch money, which the Chiefs gladly did to the New York Jets last week.

The Chiefs have another chance to rebuild fans’ confidence in the team this Sunday when they take on the hapless Atlanta Falcons.

We’ll see how quickly new addition wide receiver Josh Downs can get in the mix and start making his presence felt on the field. If so, we may continue to see the fans’ confidence rise if Kansas City can go on a winning streak.

Regardless. As long as we can keep winning games, I suspect this confidence number will grow right along with it.

Can the Chiefs still win the division?

While it’s nowhere near the realm of possibility that Denver drops a couple of games in the coming weeks, their next five games are not exactly a murderer’s row of competition. The Denver Broncos play the Las Vegas Raiders twice, and the New York Jets, the Pittsburgh Steelers, and the Miami Dolphins each once.

The Steelers are the one game where I think the other team could give Denver a run for its money. And I have to admit that it feels a little dirty to be in the awkward position of cheering on the Raiders this weekend. But here we are.

I have to admit that 50% also feels about right as to whether the Chiefs can win this division. They are by no means a perfect team, but they are good enough that they could win any game they are a part of, and if a team like that gets on a roll, they can be very dangerous.

item.title: 5 biggest needs for Bears in 2027 offseason
item.description: In the bye week, @jacobinfante24 looks at the Bears’ biggest needs, as well as some 2027 draft prospects to watch.
item.content:encoded:
Heading into their Week 10 bye week, the Bears find themselves with a favorable 7-2 record and a first-place standing in the loaded NFC North. Even with the slight derailment of Caleb Williams missing three games due to injury, they are firmly positioned as one of the top teams in the NFL entering the second half of the season.

Since the Bears don’t play a game this weekend, now is as good of a time as any to look towards the future. I’m not in full mock offseason mode yet, especially since a few potential cut candidate veterans still have a lot to prove before I feel comfortable projecting who stays and who goes. But for the most part, we know what their biggest strengths and weaknesses will be heading into the 2027 offseason.

I’ll be ranking the Bears’ five biggest needs this offseason are, and I’ll include a few prospects in the 2027 NFL Draft that could be of interest in the second round. Since Chicago traded its first-round pick this year for Jeffery Simmons, highlighting potential Day 2 prospects will make up a lot of our draft coverage in the weeks and months ahead. I’ll include players ranked around the Round 2 range using the PFN Consensus Big Board, and I’ll include my own rankings for each player accordingly.

5. Offensive guard

Guard is much more of a long-term need than a short-term one, as Joe Thuney is the reigning Protector of the Year, and Jonah Jackson is playing at an All-Pro level in 2026. However, Thuney is experiencing slight regression; his 75.8 PFN OL Impact grade is a considerable dip from his 91.1 grade last year. He’ll be turning 34 years old in a few days, and if the Bears do well enough in the playoffs, it’s possible he could look to call it a career.

Obviously, the ideal scenario sees Thuney stick around in Chicago for at least another season. But the team could eventually use a long-term successor to him along its interior offensive line. I wouldn’t expect the Bears to draft a guard early this year, and they have solid depth with the likes of Luke Newman and Jordan McFadden. That said, it’s a position they could address earlier than people expect if the value is right, or if Thuney chooses to retire this offseason.

2027 draft prospects in Round 2:

  • Austin Siereveld, Ohio State (Consensus: 45; Infante: 59)
  • Cayden Green, Missouri (Consensus: 56; Infante: 58)
  • Carter Smith, Indiana (Consensus: 61; Infante: 34)
  • Evan Tengesdahl, Cincinnati (Consensus: 85; Infante: 139)

4. Linebacker

Should the Bears let go of T.J. Edwards this offseason, it would free them $8.5 million in cap space in 2027. Among 78 qualified linebackers, his 66.2 PFN LB Impact grade ranks just No. 72 at the position. They could just slide D’Marco Jackson in his place in the starting lineup next year, but there’s also a chance they could draft a linebacker early.

I’d keep an eye on speedier players at the position, as defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has emphasized the importance of speed and mobility on his defense. The 2027 draft lacks the blue-chip talent at linebacker that 2026 had in Sonny Styles and Arvell Reese, but there are a handful of solid Day 2 prospects who could be right up Chicago’s alley.

2027 draft prospects in Round 2:

  • Sammy Brown, Clemson (Consensus: 53; Infante: 40)
  • Tony Rojas, Penn State (Consensus: 78; Infante: 67)
  • Sammy Omosigho, UCLA (Consensus: 124; Infante: 81)
  • Rasheem Biles, Texas (Consensus: 183; Infante: 82)

3. Defensive end

All things considered, the Bears’ group of defensive ends has been better than I expected it would be going into 2026. Austin Booker has performed at a high level, Dayo Odeyingbo showed improvement before his injury, and Montez Sweat’s play has gotten better since Chicago traded for Jeffery Simmons. There’s still plenty of long-term uncertainty at the position, however.

The Bears will need cap space to work with in the 2027 offseason, and it’s likely that a big move will be made at defensive end to free some up. Sweat’s release would create $21 million in cap space, while Odeyingbo’s release would free up $15 million. It’s unlikely they choose to cut both, but one of them could end up as a cap casualty. At that point, Chicago would need a new edge rusher to pair with the likes of Booker, Shemar Turner, and whichever veteran they choose to keep around. Luckily for them, the 2027 draft is deep with high-floor, powerful edge rushers who fit the physical mold that Allen historically prefers in his hand-in-the-dirt defensive ends.

2027 draft prospects in Round 2:

  • Will Heldt, Clemson (Consensus: 54; Infante: 53)
  • Clev Lubin, Louisville (Consensus: 55; Infante: 66)
  • Kenyatta Jackson Jr., Ohio State (Consensus: 72; Infante: 78)
  • Matayo Uiagalelei, Oregon (Consensus: 75; Infante: 64)
  • Jordan Ross, LSU (Consensus: 80; Infante: 73)

2. Defensive tackle

The addition of Jeffery Simmons has had a massive impact on the Bears’ defense, and part of why the team was willing to give up two first-round picks for him was the fact that he recently signed an extension with the Titans. As a result, Chicago can hold onto him through 2030. His presence definitely helps the interior defensive line, but that group is otherwise pretty thin.

Grady Jarrett projects as a cap casualty with the $13.5 million the Bears would free up by releasing him. Elsewhere, they don’t have a proven long-term option at the position outside of Simmons. The likes of Neville Gallimore, Jordan van den Berg, and Jayden Loving could end up as decent depth pieces, but none of them have proven to be starting-caliber players in the NFL (at least not yet, in the case of the latter two). Adding another interior defensive force should be a priority for the Bears, and there happen to be several defensive tackle prospects I like in the Day 2 range of this 2027 draft class, even though they’ll be missing out on some of the first-round talent.

2027 draft prospects in Round 2:

  • Tavion Gadson, Kentucky (Consensus: 46; Infante: 68)
  • Ahmad Moten, Miami (FL) (Consensus: 47; Infante: 18)
  • Justin Scott, Miami (FL) (Consensus: 49; Infante: 44)
  • Bear Alexander, Oregon (Consensus: 57; Infante: 109)
  • A.J. Holmes Jr., Texas Tech (Consensus: 74; Infante: 32)

1. Cornerback

This season has been very exciting for the Bears so far, but the biggest disappointment with this team in 2026 has to be the cornerback room. Malik Muhammad has surpassed expectations as a fourth-round rookie, and Kyler Gordon’s return in the slot has been valuable, but Chicago has otherwise faced rocky play at the position along the perimeter.

Jaylon Johnson had a pick-six and shut down the Buccaneers’ offense last Sunday night, but he’s played poorly for most of the season. It’s possible the Simmons addition can help turn his season around, but with the $16 million the Bears would free up by releasing him, Johnson remains on the bubble. Tyrique Stevenson is also an impending free agent, and much like Chicago’s many secondary free agents from the 2026 offseason, it feels unlikely that the team extends him. We’ll see which cornerback prospects actually declare for the 2027 draft, but there’s a lot of good value late in Round 2 or early in Round 3 based on my current evaluations.

  • Vicari Swain, South Carolina (Consensus: 50; Infante: 99)

  • Andrew Marshall, Nebraska (Consensus: 50; Infante: 49)

item.title: A scoop and score is long overdue for the New York Jets
item.description: The Jets need some game changing plays on defense
item.content:encoded:
The Jets’ defense has had its issues in 2026, to say the least. However, there’s at least one area where they have improved. The defense as a whole has been a lot more opportunistic this year in terms of forcing fumbles.

Led by David Bailey’s five, they have forced a total of 13 fumbles. That’s already four more than the total for all of last season.

New York’s fumble luck has been a lot better too, as they’ve recovered 50 percent of all fumbles. This is much higher than their 2025 percentage, which was the second-worst in the league at 35 percent (and was actually on target to break the all-time record until they had a few over the last few weeks of the season).

Had they been closer to 50 percent last year, or 2023 when they were dead last in fumble recovery percentage, or 2022 when they were 30th, those seasons could arguably have played out very differently.

2023 in particular was particularly galling, as the Jets started 7-4 and then lost their last six as the turnovers dried up. They almost tied the all-time NFL record for the fewest defensive fumble recoveries until Carl Lawson ended a nine-game drought by recovering one with two games remaining. In the end, they only managed to recover 21 percent of fumbles by opposing offenses.

It’s often been debated how much of fumble recovery percentages are dictated by talent and how much is based on luck, with most analytical studies concluding it’s mostly luck. However, if you have a team that is hungry and hustles to the ball, has players who are particularly adept at possessing loose balls or are creating the kinds of fumbles which are more likely to be recovered by the defense, this obviously has an effect on some level.

Regardless, at least the Jets have seemingly started to regress to the mean in this area. So the next question becomes when will they start to do anything impactful with these recoveries?

This Thursday marked the 14th anniversary of the last time a Jets defensive player recovered a ball off the turf and returned it for a touchdown. That was Muhammad Wilkerson, on a play where Mike DeVito had forced the ball loose on a sack of Russell Wilson.

That’s a pretty remarkable statistic. Although there have only been six fumble returns for touchdowns in the first nine weeks of this NFL season, the Jets averaged over eight fumble returns per decade in the 80’s, 90’s and 2000’s. Doesn’t it feel like they’re long overdue?

Wilkerson’s touchdown was not actually the last defensive fumble return for a touchdown by the Jets. Jamal Adams officially owns that distinction, on a memorable play where he ripped the ball out of Daniel Jones’ hands and ran it in. He therefore didn’t recover it off the ground, so it wasn’t a conventional scoop and score.

Even this was a far-too-long seven years ago.

Since 2012, the Jets have also scored three other touchdowns on fumbles but two (Matt Slauson and Charone Peake) were on offense, and the other was a muffed punt recovered in the end zone by Art Maulet. Again, none of these was in the past seven years.

The Jets’ last defensive touchdown was a pick-six by Jermaine Johnson and that one dates back to 2023.

It feels like a scoop and score is exactly the kind of momentum-shifting play that has been lacking ever since Aaron Glenn took over as head coach. It’s the kind of thing that could give them a chance to upset a favored opponent, which is something Glenn’s team probably needs to do a couple of times between now and the end of the season if he wants to mount a strong enough case to return for a third year.

With Bailey in particular doing a good job of creating these opportunities, perhaps this could be something that happens sooner rather than later.

Now we’ve written about this, perhaps this will manifest a Jets fumble return for a touchdown in an upcoming game. Otherwise, we’ll be writing about how long it was since Wilkerson’s touchdown again in a few seasons…

item.title: Cleveland Browns vs. Houston Texans: 2 key matchups to watch on Sunday
item.description: Denzel Ward vs. Nico Collins and Denzel Boston vs. Derek Stingley Jr. outcomes could determine who goes home a winner.
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns host the Houston Texans on Sunday in a game with actual playoff implications for both teams.

Cleveland is currently tied with the New England Patriots for the final playoff spot in the AFC, but the Patriots hold the edge with a 5-1 record in the conference. The Browns already have three conference losses, so a fourth one on Sunday would put a major dent in their playoff hopes and also give the Texans the tiebreaker.

But if the Browns pick up the win? Then they will enter the bye week with a 45 percent chance of making the playoffs, according to The Athletic’s playoff simulator, which means meaningful football will be on the docket for the rest of the season.

While much of the focus of Sunday’s game will be on how Cleveland’s offensive line can keep Houston’s pass rush, which comes into the game tied for first in the league with 29 sacks, away from quarterback Deshaun Watson, who has taken a league-high 33 sacks, there are other matchups to watch.

Here are two in particular to keep an eye on, according to Pro Football Focus.

Houston WR Nico Collins vs. Cleveland CB Denzel Ward

Collins is second on the Texans in receptions (28), and first in receiving yards (384) and receiving touchdowns (4). But he hasn’t had an explosive game since early October when he torched the Dallas Cowboys with seven receptions for 118 yards and two touchdowns. 

Ward, meanwhile, is putting together his standard season of high-level play, which makes for a good matchup, according to PFF:

Collins has missed time in 2026 but has been tremendously dynamic as usual when healthy. He’s notched an 82.8 PFF receiving grade along with 2.10 yards per route run, with 2026 marking his fourth straight season with numbers reaching those thresholds. Further, Collins’ 82.4% contested catch rate is the third-best among receivers with 35 or more targets.

Ward has starred from the outset this season, earning a 72.0-plus PFF coverage grade in all but one game throughout the year. He’s permitted just 18 catches for 129 yards across 349 coverage snaps, numbers that warrant being a first-team All-Pro through the midway point of 2026.

These two standouts haven’t gone head-to-head in a game since the 2023 postseason, although Ward has generally had Collins’ number. Collins has been held to two catches for 53 yards over their three games facing one another, with Ward winning 75% of the reps in terms of being charted as open.

Cleveland WR Denzel Boston vs. Houston CB Derek Stingley Jr.

Boston came close to his first 100-yard receiving day last week against the New Orleans Saints (six receptions for 98 yards), and leads all rookies in receiving yards (507).

Stingley is currently going through a down year, so if Boston can play through his toe injury, this could be an area for the Browns to exploit, according to PFF:

Collins vs. Ward is the meeting of two longtime great players, but Boston vs. Stingley represents the next generation of potential showstopping receiver-corner battles.

Boston looks like the frontrunner for Offensive Rookie of the Year through the season’s midway point. He’s collected a 70.3 PFF receiving grade while averaging 1.55 yards per route run. Likewise, Boston’s 5.0 yards after the catch per reception sit in the 74th percentile.

Like the rest of Houston’s regressing defense, Stingley has had some trouble this season — producing a career-low 65.3 PFF receiving grade with a 92.4 passer rating allowed. Although the All-Pro has let up 65-plus yards in three separate games, he’s also broken up five passes.

Boston has dealt with a toe injury in practice but indicated he expects to play on Sunday. That means we should be treated to a physical showdown between the big-frame rookie and one of the game’s top defensive backs over the last few seasons.

The Browns have an opportunity on Sunday to go into their bye week on a positive note and come out on the other side with a legitimate chance to stay in the playoff race. 

And these two matchups could determine who is celebrating come Monday morning.

item.title: 49ers Mailbag: Playoffs, parity, and Connor Colby
item.description: Alot of questions heading into Week 10. Like, what’s up with all this parity? And “Why is Brandon Aiyuk still there?”
item.content:encoded:
Well, it’s always funnier when the 49ers beat the Cowboys. And it’s always better when we have a mailbag before a 49ers game.

So I found out I have this nifty little tool that lets me link your comments to my Niners Nation Feed post directly. It’s pretty neat, so I’m using it for this. Our mailbag requests come during the week in The Feed. I go through comments, good and/or bad, and pick a few to respond to. Those I don’t respond to are probably because I don’t have a witty-enough response or something I simply didn’t have time for (the final 53-man roster at season’s end is a great question, but I don’t even want to rack my brain on that one). Basically, it’s not you, it’s me.

All you need to do is see my mailbag post on The Feed and then make a comment about what we should talk about! We had a lot of questions this week. I’ll try to answer some of them:

I don’t mind parity; I do think it’s being taken a biiiiit too far, however. I’m against a top team having a first pick in the draft—that’s where you get all the NBA controversies with lotteries and such. That said NBA draft “lottery” was originally implemented to prevent all-out tanking, but somehow elite prospects get picked up by specific teams, defying the odds.

Here’s what I WOULD like. I agree with your salary cap worries, but I don’t think it should be removed—instead, adjusted. Several companies that have remote workers adjust salaries based on cost of living. For example, I live in Seattle, Washington, so my salary for a position would be significantly higher than someone living in Jackpot, Nevada. I think income tax can be a key decision-maker for players, and teams that have to deal with income taxes should adjust accordingly. Washington has no income tax; California does. So adjust the salary cap accordingly based on the tax structure of that team’s state. How do you do this? I have no idea. I am the worst at numbers.

My other suggestion for the salary cap is that for any player drafted by a team who accrues x years on that team and is up for an extension, a percentage of their new deal doesn’t count against the salary cap. This lets them get the deal they want without crippling the team. This also rewards teams for drafting well rather than penalizing them. It’s like a franchise tag you can use once a year on a newly signed contract. Oftentimes, players don’t want to leave their team, but the business side of things gets in the way, and the team can only offer so much. Having a rule like this in effect would create roster consistency and ensure the talent gets the salary they deserve. You can go even further, like any pick in the second round-on, while the first round has the fifth-year option.

The whole idea is that teams are rewarded for investing their resources and time into a prospect rather than the player’s contract being up and priced out of whatever team wants to keep them.

Probably the Minnesota Vikings now that Kirk Cousins is back. I’m still traumatized by his last game against the 49ers in the purple back in 2023. Cousins went 35-for-45 (77 percent completions), for 378 yards, two touchdowns, and a single interception.

You know that game better for this stupid Steve Wilks call. This game was where the murmurs of Wilks’ incompetence pretty much spilled out into screaming rants. After this game, he left the booth and came to the sidelines to call games. You know how that season turned out. Yes, the 49ers went to the Super Bowl, but those defensive formations, man.

So looking back, Kirk Cousins back on the Vikings scares me. If not for that trade this week, I’d probably lean towards the Chicago Bears, but the Vikings are my pick.

I don’t get it at this point. He’s reinstated, and the 49ers have two weeks. I’ve been on the 49ers’ side for all of this until right now, when I’m wondering why they just don’t cut the cord. My guess is they don’t want to cut him and have him go to a team they may face in two weeks. I doubt he’s in football shape, but I also wonder what he could give the Seahawks and/or Vikings if he signed with them. Keeping him for two weeks makes any signing more of a crunch.

But then he could go to the Rams? I just don’t know what the 49ers are doing right now. Get it over with already.

Here’s a nice stat that will help you figure this out:

58.1…yet somehow the 49ers are still standing. I think Colby is surrounded by talent (hey there, Colton McKivitz), but he’s clearly the weak link of the offensive line at left guard. The rest of the line has been doing a fine job. Now that said, can he get better? I think so. This is only his second season, and it’s still an improvement over last year.

If the 49ers look to add another guard in the draft (one can wish upon a star), I hope they lock up Dominick Puni so they have some consistency on that line. I don’t think Colby is horrible (remember Erik Pears? THAT was bad), but we need to see how he develops for the rest of the year. The last thing we need is Jeffery Simmons lined up against him in the playoffs.

I’d say the 2023 team was maybe more balanced—once they figured their decorum out. The 2023 team had that losing streak to the Vikings and Bengals and looked awful. I don’t know what they did to turn it around, but whatever it was, it got them to the Super Bowl. The issue with the 2023 team was defensive coaching (Steve Wilks was defensive coordinator) and Brock Purdy’s inexperience (which he mitigated well).

The 2026 team is balanced, but I need to see more from the defense. I don’t mind the pass rush having a hard time sacking the quarterback, so long as the secondary is making pass-catchers pay for catching the ball. Sure, the Raiders had dial-a-turnovers against the 49ers, but that’s an anomaly. A lot of those turnovers (like the end zone fumble) are simply not going to happen most of the time. The stats will tell me otherwise, as the 49ers defense is one of the better defenses in the league (especially against the run), but both the Falcons game and the Raiders game have me questioning the pass rush. Since we got Nick Bosa back and DeForest Buckner returned, I hope that changes as things gel.

That sounds like something El Shorts would do. I wonder what ever happened to that guy? He was a good dude.

Whichever one eliminates the team that is the worst matchup for the 49ers. The Minnesota Vikings did the 49ers fans a favor in 2019 by knocking the New Orleans Saints out, and that was the team I thought would give the 49ers the most headaches (though the Saleh defense showed itself against the Packers at the end).

If I have to look at what’s there, I’d probably just enjoy Giants-Vikings and watching the Giants knock the Vikings out. Since the NFC East is not very good this year, that would provide some pretty good comedy. As far as a game, Bears-Packers would be great, since it removes one of the threats to the 49ers. Then again, Bears-Rams would be nice, but I don’t know who I’d want to win that one.

So specifically wide receivers, I’m going to go with De’Zhaun Stribling, Mike Evans, Jordan Watkins, Brandin Cooks, Deebo Samuel, and Keenan Allen. I think once Stribling is good to go and Evans returns to the field, Jacob Cowing could be the odd man out. I’d put Cooks on punt returns and Watkins/Samuel on Kickoff returns.

I think we’ve seen what Cowing is capable of, and all I see is bad decisions, bad ball security, and quitting on plays (like Brock Purdy’s interception against the Falcons). He’s been with the team long enough (drafted in 2024) and there just hasn’t been anything to “wow” me.

Unfortunately, the 49ers wide receivers aren’t getting any younger, so maybe cutting him would be a bad idea. I just don’t see how he can play with who the 49ers have.

I suck at chess. It’s a silly game. I’ll own you in Life, though.

No, but you can. That could be a great feed topic for you to rank the best commenters. I don’t want to get involved playing favorites.

item.title: Question of the Day: How far do Bears have to go for you to be satisfied?
item.description: How far do the Chicago Bears need to make it this year for you to be satisfied with their season? Sound off!
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears have hit the bye at 7-2 and are sitting in first place of the gauntlet NFC North. The Bears have a tough second-half schedule but certainly appear to be headed to the playoffs for the second consecutive year.

Last season, the Bears won the division, won their first playoff game in 15 years, and they were an eyelash away from reaching the NFC Championship Game. I think 99% of Bears fans, after the sting of the Rams loss wore off, were very pleased with the results of the 2025 season, even if they lost the last game they played.

This year, at approximately the midway point in the season, the Bears are at or near the top of everyone’s list of a true Super Bowl contender. With more success comes more expectations.

How far do Bears have to go for you to be satisfied with their season?

I think as fans, when the team is building something, we want to see them improve upon the previous season. Since there were only four teams that had more postseason success than Chicago, there isn’t a ton of room to improve. That being said, I think Bears fans and NFL media around the country expect the Bears to be better than they were in 2025.

Answer: I think the first obvious step is that for any level of satisfaction to be reached, the Bears have to be one of the last four remaining teams in the NFL. That’s a lofty thing to say, but I think it’s fair. I think if the Bears make the playoffs but lose in the Wild Card or Divisional round, there will be plenty of disappointment with the fan base. Yes, fans will be excited that the Bears made the playoffs in back-to-back seasons for the first time since 2005 and 2006, but that won’t be good enough. Even if the Bears win a playoff game in back-to-back seasons, it’ll be the first time they’ve done that since 1984 and 1985, but even then, that won’t be good enough.

I think for some fans, reaching the NFC Championship Game will be enough. If the San Francisco 49ers are the 1 seed and the Bears go on the road and lose in that game, there will be a certain level of satisfaction, but I still don’t think that’s enough.

I think the Bears need to reach the Super Bowl for me to walk away feeling excited without too much disappointment. Obviously, I want them to win, but if Josh Allen climbs the mountaintop and beats the Bears and wins the Super Bowl, am I going to be freaking out? No, I just think the Bears will be ready to take the next step in 2027.

What say you, Bears fans? How far do the Bears have to go this year for you to be content with their season? Is it Super Bowl or bust, like it is for Bill Zimmerman? Is it the Lombardi Trophy? Or is a lower level of success good enough for you? Sound off in the comments below!

item.title: Jared Goff takes 1-3 career record vs. Patriots into Germany game
item.description: For his career, Lions quarterback Jared Goff has a record of 101-67-1 as a starter.
item.content:encoded:
For his career, Lions quarterback Jared Goff has a record of 101-67-1 as a starter. That's a 59.7-percent win rate.

Against the Patriots, Goff is 1-3. That's a 25-percent win rate.

In those four games, Goff has two touchdown passes and five interceptions.

Sunday's game in Germany will be the first one against the Patriots with a coach other than Bill Belichick. Goff has never faced current Patriots coach Mike Vrabel; during Goff's time as a starter with the Rams and Lions and Vrabel's tenure with the Titans, their two teams never crossed paths.

Goff's first loss to New England came in 2016, in his third career start. The Patriots won, 26-10. Two years later, New England beat Goff and the Rams in the Super Bowl, 13-3.

In 2020, the Patriots beat Goff and the Rams, 24-3. In 2022, the Patriots beat Goff and the Lions, 29-0.

Sunday's game is consequential for both teams. The 6-2 Lions are caught in a cluster of four NFC North teams that all have six or more wins. The Patriots, at 5-4, are fading in the AFC East race and could be scrambling to secure a wild-card spot.

item.title: Giants know why Dominic Zvada is missing kicks; now, can they fix it?
item.description: Rookie kicker’s struggles have been costly. How long can the Giants wait as he tries to fix the technique issue?
item.content:encoded:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh has steadfastly stood by rookie placekicker Dominic Zvada through Zvada’s ups and downs this season, which have included too many costly misses.

Harbaugh continued to do so after Zvada’s latest miss, an extra-point distance 33-yarder in what became a three-point loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday night.

“You can’t, as soon as a guy doesn’t make a play, start firing people left and right. Especially your kicker who’s a rookie,” Harbaugh said. “So, I’m confident he’s going to become a good kicker. I mean, at some point in time, if it doesn’t happen, it doesn’t happen. But I’m not going to panic halfway through the season when a guy’s made a bunch of kicks, if that’s what you’re inferring we should be doing. We’re just not going to knee jerk it like that. He’s going to make kicks. He’s going to make a lot of kicks. I believe in him. I think he’s really good and really talented. We’re going to give him an opportunity to do it, and it’s up to him to do it.“

Turns out, all six of Zvada’s misses this season — three pushed wide right and three yanked wide left — have come from the right hash.

“There’s a technique issue there with his plant foot that we’re kind of looking at,” Harbaugh said on Friday. “And he needs to clean that up from a consistency standpoint. He knows that. Popped up again in that one kick there. There is an issue on the right hash, no question.”

Zvada was tremendous all spring and summer, beating out Ben Sauls for the placekicking job. He started the season 9-for-9, but has made just 8 of 14 kicks since.

It is fair to say that Zvada’s struggles were critical parts of why the Giants tied and lost games to the Commanders, rather than winning both games. He missed three kicks in the tie to Washington in Week 5, and his miss Thursday came in a 3-point loss.

It is also fair to wonder if Zvada’s struggles have impacted some of Harbaugh’s decisions. The Giants punted three times inside Washington territory Thursday night — from the 37-, 41- and 46-yard lines. Two of those kicks would have come from inside 60 yards, where the Giants have already asked Zvada to kick nine times this season.

Maybe the play-calling that led to the punts would have been different if the Giants truly had faith in Zvada. Or, maybe they would have allowed him to try those kicks.

“Well, let’s look at the distances. Why don’t you go back and give me the distances. I don’t have it in front of me. What were those field goals have been? They were like high 50s, weren’t they? 55 plus,” Harbaugh said. “It’s kind of a risk-reward. I’m not saying that he can’t make those kicks, but it’s a windy night and it’s a field position game in some ways. It’s a big risk there, too. Sometimes it’s better to play a field position game.

“So those were toss up kind of calls probably at least, probably leaning toward punting, but I’m not saying we shouldn’t have gone for them or couldn’t have kicked them either way. The one question is, “should you have gone for it?” The next question is, “should you have kicked the field goals?” That’s the follow-up question. I don’t know. The other question could have been if we’d have missed the field goal, maybe you should have punted it down in there and played the field position game. So they’re all kind of coin flip type of decisions.”

Here is how the analytics saw each of the three situations in which the Giants chose to punt rather than try the field or go for the first down:

Giants 0, Commanders 0
Fourth-and-7 at the Washington 37, Q1 11:28

Commanders 17, Giants 14
Fourth-and-3 at the Washington 46, Q4 14:15

Giants 21, Commanders 17
Fourth-and-5 at the Washington 41, Q4 1:54

The point here isn’t to debate which decisions Harbaugh made correctly, and which he didn’t. Though discussing that is certainly fair game. The point is that Zvada’s continued misses are complicating the decision-making and costing the Giants points that are probably costing them games.

In an NFC East race that seems likely to go down to the wire, and where every decision, every made or missed kick, everything that happens in the margins of an NFL game, could end up making the difference how much rope can the Giants give Zvada to figure it out?

item.title: How has Sean McVay and the Rams done against rookie quarterbacks?
item.description: Sean McVay and the Rams typically beat rookie QB’s and more NFL news
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams under Sean McVay are 9-2 against rookie quarterbacks and that could be bad news for Carson Beck and the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday. It also could be an awesome opportunity for Beck to show up the Rams and fellow rookie Ty Simpson who will be on the sidelines.

If Beck wins, then that’d be a great start to a NFL career. If Beck loses against Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald, then perhaps that was to be expected.

We’ll have to tune in on Sunday to see Beck is another win for the Rams against rookie signal callers, or if he earns the tough win.

How have rookie QBs fared historically vs. Sean McVay and the Rams? (ramswire)

“Historically, rookie quarterbacks have struggled against the Rams. The odds are against Beck to buck that trend; Arizona is a 9.5-point underdog in this game, making the Rams heavy favorites despite being on the road

Rookie QB stats vs. Rams since 2017

With McVay as the head coach, the Rams are 9-2 against rookie quarterbacks, according to Stathead. The only two rookies to beat the Rams were Caleb Williams in 2024 and Tua Tagovailoa in 2020. Tagovailoa only threw for 93 yards and one touchdown in that shocking win against Jared Goff and the Rams, while Williams had just 157 yards and a score in the Bears‘ 24-18 win over Los Angeles in 2024.“

Week 10 picks: Experts predict Rams won’t get upset by Cardinals again (sports.yahoo)

“The Los Angeles Rams head into Week 10 battered and bruised, but with a winning record for the first time all season. They’ll also take on an Arizona Cardinals team that upset them in Week 6. A win would help the Rams keep pace for the Wild Card as well as deliver the team’s first divisional win in 2026.

It’ll be an interesting showdown given how well the Rams defense performed in Week 9 with Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett finally on the field together, especially given they’ll take on rookie quarterback Carson Beck and a similarly-injured Cardinals offense. Arizona is also without running back Jeremiyah Love and receiver Michael Wilson. The Rams, meanwhile, won’t have Puka Nacua, Davante Adams or Jordan Whittington in this game.

NFL experts are not expecting an upset this time around. Los Angeles received all 52 picks across seven major outlets, with no analyst picking the Cardinals.“

Los Angeles Rams Announce Myles Garrett Decision Amid Significant Updates (heavy.com)

““Guys that will be DNPs: Myles Garrett. He’ll be questionable for the game. He’s feeling good. It’s more of just getting him feeling as good as possible. He’s had a really good week, played a bunch of snaps, and expect him to be able to build on that. But we’re being smart with him,” McVay told reporters on November 13. “Steve Avila will be listed as out with his hamstring. Trent McDuffie and Kam Curl will both be limited for practice today and listed as questionable. And then, Terrance Ferguson will be out for the game as well.”

The most encouraging sign of Garrett’s status for Sunday is that he took the podium to speak with the media to close out the week.“

Rams’ Myles Garrett Among Multiple Questionable Players for Week 10 (sports.yahoo)

“Garrett has been on the injury report with a knee ailment, which limited him on both Wednesday and Thursday. Per Rams reporter Stu Jackson, the defensive end is now questionable.

In addition to Garrett, cornerback Trent McDuffie and safety Kam Curl are also questionable.

McVay did state that he expects Garrett to play and “feels good” about Curl, which may likely lead to both suiting up for the Cardinals matchup. However, McDuffie is more of a worry, and his response over the weekend to working out will determine if he can play.“

Rams’ Myles Garrett expected to play at Arizona despite missing practice (mymotherlode)

“Garrett was largely pleased with his performance, in which he played 61.5% of the defensive snaps, apart from needing to build up his endurance and address what he felt was a slow get-off time.

“I’m sure Next Gen or PFF or somebody would tell me it wasn’t too bad,” Garrett said. “It felt terrible to me.”

McDuffie is dealing with a back injury that forced him to miss the Rams’ third straight win last week, getting them over .500 for the first time this season at 5-4. McVay expressed optimism he would be able to play, provided McDuffie felt good coming out of Friday’s workout.

“He was rolling, you know, doing a lot of good stuff yesterday,” McVay said.

The ongoing issues with the Rams’ two marquee offseason acquisitions is indicative of their larger injury crisis that has threatened a campaign that began with them as Super Bowl betting favorites. Los Angeles is so beat up that star wide receiver Puka Nacua was placed on injured reserve Thursday to free up a roster spot, a reversal from what McVay had indicated earlier in the week when he cited the limited number of IR slots remaining to be able to bring players back later in the season.

“Some things changed where we needed that spot because of all the moving pieces,” said McVay, while adding that nothing has changed with the timeline for Nacua’s return from knee and toe injuries.“

Rams’ $71 million injury nightmare among NFL’s worst (sports.yah00)

“The Rams have watched a parade of Pro Bowlers, All-Pros and established starters limp into the training room this season, including Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, Davante Adamsand Puka Nacua.

Garrett, the two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year, finally returned in Week 9 after undergoing knee surgery. Meanwhile, Watson is lost for the season, Adams remains sidelined with a hamstring injury, and Nacua is dealing with knee ligament sprains and turf toe.

It’s enough to make the Rams’ medical staff consider asking for overtime pay.

Believe it or not, the Rams aren’t even the most injured team in California, at least according to RotoWire’s formula.“

FAA flight debacle could disrupt Rams, Chargers, 49ers; NFL responds (nypost)

“The Rams have spent all week preparing for the Cardinals. Now, an unprecedented travel nightmare could force them to prepare for a road trip of an entirely different kind.

A nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday afternoon has thrown weekend travel plans into chaos, potentially affecting several NFL teams scheduled to fly to their respective games Saturday.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the shutdown about 1:15 p.m. PT, citing a communications issue affecting air traffic control centers across the country.“

Rams injury report: Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie questionable vs. Cardinals (ramswire)

item.title: What the numbers say about a winner in Cowboys vs 49ers
item.description: Breaking down the numbers for the Cowboys and 49ers game
item.content:encoded:
Every week, we’ll examine the numbers behind the next opponent on the schedule. Looking at the recent numbers and trends for each team, we’ll add it all up to see which squad may have the edge. This week, the 4-5 Dallas Cowboys take on the 7-1 San Francisco 49ers.

Cowboys key stats from last week

Dak Prescott threw for 335 yards, two touchdowns and finished with a passer rating of 114.2. He finished the game with a four-play, 65-yard game winning touchdown drive in just 29 seconds.

CeeDee Lamb led the team with another massive performance through the air. He racked up an astonishing 195 receiving yards and one touchdown, also fumbling once on an odd play.

Javonte Williams and Tyler Goodson finished with a combined 32 carries and 178 yards on the ground.

Despite these incredible numbers, the Cowboys offense failed to convert yards into points throughout the day. Held back by turnovers and penalties, it took a fantastic one-handed catch from Ryan Flournoy in the waning moments of the game to sneak out of Indianapolis with a win.

49ers key stats from last week

Brock Purdy and the 49ers finished last week with 232 passing yards, two passing touchdowns, and one interception. Purdy also rushed for 40 yards and converted a touchdown with his legs.

Kaelon Black outrushed Christian McCaffrey on seven less rushing attempts, finishing with 70 yards. McCaffrey remains this biggest threat, however, finishing with 87 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns.

The 49ers defense limited Las Vegas to just 24 rushing yards on their way to a 38-17 rout of the Silver and Black. They forced three interceptions, including one pick-six.

The formula for San Francisco remains the same after all these years – play efficient offense and let the physical defense swing the game.

Call an aggressively smart game

The Cowboys are going to have to put up points. San Francisco just has too many weapons offensively, especially in the backfield, for this defense to shut them down for 60 minutes. It’s extremely unlikely this turns into a defensive fist fight.

With that in mind, this should be the proper week to bust out the gutsy calls. 4th and inches at your own 40? Sounds like a QB sneak to me. Dallas can choose to kick a 57-yard field goal or they can go for it on 4th and 2. This is one time where it’s ok to skip leg day. Send out the offense and attack.

Brian Schottenheimer needs to understand what’s at stake here. Nobody expects the Cowboys to win, but a win has the potential to turn this entire season into something meaningful. Call this game like your back is against the wall and your football life is on the line. It’s going to take a gutsy performance from every player and every coach this week if the Cowboys are to stand a chance.

What do the numbers mean?

The Cowboys are one of the worst rushing defenses in the NFL. The 49ers possess one of the best rushing attacks, utilizing two backs and a scheme where you never know where the ball is going to go. Dallas is also one of the league’s worst third-down defenses while the 49ers convert at a higher rate than almost every team. The 49ers are clearly the better team, especially when looking at their offense against the Cowboys defense.

Yet the FanDuel line is only a 4.5 point spread. This tells me that the line setters understand that Dallas has the talent in the building to keep up and win a game against the 49ers. It just takes one week for everything to come together and see an explosion from this Cowboys team. We’ve yet to see it in 2026, however.

If Dallas is to stand a chance this week, they’ll need to finally put together a complete performance for the first time this season. They’ll need to play mistake-free football while making the plays on both sides of the ball that they just haven’t done often enough in 2026. And don’t sleep on the special teams performance playing an important role in the field position battle.

If the Cowboys put out their best performance on 2026 by playing mistake free football, scoring touchdowns instead of field goals, and winning the turnover differential, I give them a 40-50% chance at winning this game.

But from everything we’ve seen, the Cowboys do not play mistake free football. They are unable to consistently get stops on defense, especially against good teams with good rushing attacks. This team has also played several games where the offense has struggled to put points on the board. To top it off, the head coach has made far too many questionable decisions that have directly impacted the results of these games.

The Cowboys are the ultimate wild card this week. Put it all together and have a chance to steal a tough win. Play the same brand of football we’ve seen far too often this season, and this could be a multiple score loss. This is the game that determines the team they’ll be the rest of the season.

item.title: 3-Point Stance: Defense could be a roadblock in Patriots’ playoff pursuit
item.description: A failing defense cannot lead an injured offense.
item.content:encoded:
Last week, I wrote that the New England Patriots shouldn’t preemptively deal an impact player at the NFL trade deadline amid defensive players Christian Barmore and Carlton Davis reportedly being available for trade.

Ultimately, the Patriots didn’t make any transactions on Tuesday.

Although I cited the offseason as a better time to move either defender, I noted the defense’s encouraging Week Eight performance against the now 1-7 Miami Dolphins as a potential turning point for what has largely been an underwhelming and injured unit through the first half of the season.

That didn’t stick.

It’s hard not to be concerned about New England’s defense after last Sunday’s deflating performance against the Green Bay Packers. Those reservations are especially warranted when the Patriots’ most expensive cornerback room in the league allows two receivers, Matthew Golden and Christian Watson, to combine for 335 yards and two touchdowns, with each logging career highs.

All-Pro Christian Gonzalez, entering 2026 on a four-year, $135 million contract extension, allowed 10 receptions for 187 yards, per NextGen Stats.

“I’m a Christian Gonzalez fan,” NFL Hall of Famer Ty Law said on WEEI’s The Greg Hill Show. “I just expect more out of him … I have never been a part of a situation in my 15-year career where a secondary played that bad … That’s unacceptable … You got the bag. You have to play better.

“I’m seeing a lot of things that aren’t right when it comes to the New England Patriots’ secondary. Where is the leadership? Where is the communication? … Is it the players or the coaching?”

After the game, Gonzalez took responsibility for his poor performance but also isn’t “too worried about it.”

“I think Christian [Gonzalez] just did it to himself,” two-time Super Bowl champion Logan Ryan said on the Up & Adams Show. “I loved his comment … He said, ‘Hey, I’m allowed to have a bad day. I had a bad day.’ He doesn’t have a lot of them, and that’s going to happen. Watson and Golden are different [types of receivers] … He had to deal with them both.

“Part of being a number one corner is that you have to guard whatever comes out there … Credit to what Green Bay did, but I think mentally he was in his head. He had a slow start, and [then] it continued … That’s the life of being a number one cornerback. You have to bounce back, and I think he will.”

Head coach Mike Vrabel acknowledged that he expects more from Gonzalez while emphasizing that the rest of the defense must improve overall.

Gonzalez’s struggles are surprising, but the organization paid him for a reason. Another performance like that would be an outlier.

Still, his shortcomings highlight an underlying factor that has seen a steady decline in not only Gonzalez’s play but also the inconsistencies of the defense.

A lack of execution

Over the past week, Patriots defenders across multiple positional groups have cited execution as something to improve upon.

Veteran safety Kevin Byard frequently alluded to that sentiment when discussing the Packers’ explosive plays.

“We just didn’t execute enough,” Byard said on Sunday. “We knew that was going to be the key to the game, eliminating the big play, and we didn’t do good enough today at all. We all have to be better.”

Linebacker and captain Robert Spillane emphasized a similar message Wednesday on The Greg Hill Show, stressing the importance of playing complementary football ahead of Sunday’s matchup against the Detroit Lions, whose offense shares similarities with Green Bay’s.

“You put pressure on [Jared Goff] by stopping the run early, by forcing third-and-long passing situations, by being up on the scoreboard, by starting fast as a team, as a unit, and that’s all three phases. I think it’s really a collection of how we play as a team to get that done.”

What does that execution come down to?

It encompasses everything the team prepares for.

Against the Packers, it was schematic and assignment breakdowns. Against the Chicago Bears in Week Seven, it was a lack of physicality.

The defense allowed Chicago to notch 30 points on the evening and score on six of its nine offensive drives. Poor tackling plagued the unit throughout the game, giving up 161 yards after the catch.

Vrabel’s defense appeared a step behind, exemplifying symptoms of a Super Bowl hangover.

Following Sunday night’s loss, outside questions emerged about whether the lack of execution stems from a downward shift in team culture and energy nine months removed from the franchise’s championship appearance.

When speaking with reporters in the locker room, wide receiver Mack Hollins said that players content with New England’s performance are “probably not meant for this team,” while DeMario Douglas called for more energy and support from each unit on the sideline. Vrabel echoed the need for better execution on Monday, specifically addressing Gonzalez’s lackluster performance, explaining that “you can’t take a nap in this league.”

“You just can’t take a play off or think that they’re not going to challenge or throw the ball at you,” he said. “That’s it. You can’t think that you’re going to not draw attention.”

Vrabel, however, views it as a preparation issue, seeing Hollins’ view and his comments about wanting players who want to be with the team as a reminder of the standards required to build the program he envisions.

“Whatever reps we get, we have to make them count,” Vrabel said. ”We have to understand, if it’s a jog through, how we show the details of the play and make sure that we understand that.“

Regardless of the state of the team’s culture, poor execution and a lack of physicality are capping a defense that was slated to build on last season’s performance, ranking No. 4 in scoring defense.

Healthier defense, underperforming results

Statistically, the defense has played better while dealing with injuries compared to finally fielding a healthy starting group.

Over the last three games, New England is giving up an average of 31.3 points per game, an increase from 18.8 through the first six contests.

Squaring off with the Dolphins in Miami, things were trending upward as the divisional foes managed only five first downs in 10 offensive series.

For reference, the game marked the first time the starting cornerback trio of Gonzalez, Carlton Davis and Marcus Jones all played together since Week Three. While Davis is ruled out for Sunday with a knee injury, the defense is still nearly whole.

So far this season, the defense ranks 31st against under-center snaps and 32nd when facing early-down play-action. Their corrections against a Lions offense that frequently operates under center and has plenty of success running one of the highest play-action rates in the league.

Offense hampered by injuries

With so many injuries, the Patriots’ offense hasn’t established a rhythm all season. They simply haven’t had the pieces.

Although A.J. Brown, Rhamondre Stevenson and Reggie Gilliam were limited in practice this week, New England only recently welcomed Mack Hollins back to the lineup. The Patriots also remain without Alijah Vera-Tucker, Romeo Doubs, TreVeyon Henderson and Mike Onwenu (potentially sidelined for the season), each potentially sidelined for the season, while Hunter Henry continues to play banged up.

Even if a select few of those names return against Detroit, the defense needs to elevate its play to help New England get back in the win column consistently by keeping the offense in scoring range.

The Patriots are still 5-4 and in the playoff picture, but with a tough rest-of-season schedule and the Houston Texans sneaking into the playoff bubble, things need to turn around swiftly.

item.title: 5 questions with Pride of Detroit: How will the Lions attack Drake Maye?
item.description: We spoke with SB Nation’s Lions blog about the upcoming Patriots opponent.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots are taking on an unfamiliar opponent in an unfamiliar location this week. Playing its first ever game in the German city of Munich, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will face a Detroit Lions squad it hasn’t gone up against since 2022 — three years prior to Vrabel’s arrival.

So, to find out more about the Lions, we spoke with Ryan Mathews of Pats Pulpit’s sister site Pride of Detroit, the SB Nation community for all things Lions.

1. The Lions have been one of the least efficient coverage teams in the league, but their pass rush has been ferocious. Do you think Detroit’s pass rush is enough to keep Drake Maye from playing more like he did in October than he did last week?

To answer that, we need to adjust one premise ever so slightly: Detroit’s pass rush is more very good than dominant, and its back-end coverage is still where Lions fans want to believe in the progress that’s been made over the past four games. The Lions sit seventh in the NFL in both pressure rate (41.2% of 354 dropbacks) and sacks (27), yet opposing offenses are still averaging 0.143 EPA per dropback against them—the fourth-worst mark in the league. However, over the last four games, the Lions are averaging 0.016 EPA per dropback, which has them ranked 20th — improvement!

Drake Maye is going to be their biggest test since Jordan Love came to Ford Field in Week 7. Love thrives on pushing the ball down the field to create big plays, and Detroit’s defense did a commendable job keeping him in check, relatively speaking. He had 10 deep pass attempts, the most among quarterbacks in Week 7, and his average depth of target was 10.9 yards, but his yards per attempt (6.09) ranked 21st and his pass success rate ranked 26th.

Detroit’s defense pressured Love on 17 of his dropbacks in that game, and that played a key role in putting a lid on the deep-passing attack, so they’re going to need to keep the pressure on Maye to get similar results from their secondary.

2. The Lions have one of the deepest groups of skill players in the NFL. Has anyone managed to slow this group down, and if so, how? And would playing man coverage against them be foolish?

Detroit’s skill position players do run deep. Be it Jameson Williams’ speed, Amon-Ra St. Brown or Sam LaPorta’s craftiness in their route running and understanding of zone coverage, or Jahmyr Gibbs’ ability to do it all, they have plenty of ways to test opposing defenses.

Interestingly enough, Jared Goff ranks fourth out of 33 qualifying quarterbacks in EPA/dropback both against zone (0.194) and man (0.304) coverage — granted he’s only registered 29 dropbacks against man coverage per SumerSports — so it’s going to be interesting to see if New England sticks to their guns and plays as much man as they normally do.

3. Jahmyr Gibbs’ speed is the headliner when discussing the talented running back, but what else has allowed the Lions’ ground game to be so successful?

Gibbs’ speed doesn’t show up directly in the box score, but the underlying rushing metrics point to his contact balance and elusiveness as major drivers of Detroit’s ground attack. Across 177 carries for 847 yards (4.79 yards per carry) and nine touchdowns, Gibbs has forced 53 missed tackles (first in the NFL) and averages 3.33 yards after contact (t-12th). The explosive-play upside, generating 36.1% of his rushing yardage on carries of 12 or more yards. Backup Sione Vaki has come on as of late, offering solid physicality as a runner and a pass protector–albeit in limited action— averaging 4.5 yards per carry and 3.53 yards after contact across just 30 carries.

Schematically, Detroit leans heavily on outside zone, which accounts for 98 designed runs (excluding QB scrambles and kneels) at 4.92 yards per carry, but the offensive line has been inconsistent in their run blocking: the Lions rank 25th in stuffed rate, and it feels like the majority of that is on the big guys up front. Inside zone has actually been Detroit’s most efficient concept at 5.35 yards per carry and 0.156 EPA, largely because defenses can rarely afford to load the box against the Lions. Detroit’s facing eight or more defenders on just 15% of its 20 carries, compared to 40.8% for outside zone. Gap concepts like power and counter have struggled in small samples: ten carries for each concept, averaging 3.3 to 3.4 yards respectively.

4. Who are some underrated Lions playmakers who Patriots fans should know ahead of this game?

Looking strictly at skill-position production behind top headliners Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jahmyr Gibbs, there are three names that consistently pull their weight without always getting the national headlines.

Jameson Williams often gets typecast as a vertical threat, but he’s at his best when he’s catching passes through holes in zone coverage and making defenses pay with his speed after the catch. His elusiveness is a really underrated aspect of his game. Williams has turned 46 targets into 28 catches for 468 yards and five touchdowns so far this season, posting a strong 16.7 yards per catch — 21st in the NFL. Sam LaPorta is a reliable chain-mover over the middle, but his usage has dwindled in recent weeks ever since he publicly commented on his contract situation. Not saying, but I’m saying, you know. But maybe the most overlooked player in the Lions offense as of late is the aforementioned Sione Vaki. He’s settling well into a complementary role behind Gibbs, earning the trust of the coaching staff to the point where there have been whole series as of late where Gibbs scantily sees the field.

5.  The Lions are seen as 2.5-point favorites for this weekend’s matchup. What happened if the Patriots pull off an upset? What happened if they lost their second game in a row?

The Patriots will have pulled off the upset if their offensive line provides enough protection for Maye to air it out for big explosive plays. On defense, if they stop the Lions’ run game and force them to operate from behind the sticks in the passing game, it’s highly likely New England will leave Germany with a victory. Detroit gets the win if they pressure Maye relentlessly and he continues to turn the ball over, setting up the Lions offense with short fields to put points on the board.

The Detroit Lions fanbase is known for being great travelers. Last week against the Miami Dolphins, it felt like a home game for the players, but how will the fans travel overseas? For the first time in over a decade, the Lions are going across the pond, this time to Munich, Germany, to take on the New England Patriots.

“Real good team here. The record is not the true indication of what this team is,” said Lions head coach Dan Campbell. “There’s a number of things that go into that, that Green Bay game the other day. I mean, (Packers QB Jordan) Love was on a heater, and you know it was just kind of one of those things that happens. You look at the totality of what this team is capable of, the firepower they have, and they’re a good team. They’re dangerous, and they’re going to clean a lot of things up.”

“I think (Mike) Vrabel’s a hell of a coach and his staff. Josh (McDaniels) and those guys have done a hell of a job. Drake (Maye), he’s as good as they come getting out of the pocket right now. That’s where he’s very, very dangerous. Buying time, these five-plus-second throws, he’s dangerous, and then the skill he’s got around him. You know, three (WR DeMario Douglas) and 18 (WR Kyle Williams), and then they got (Mack) Hollins back now and the tight ends. It’s potent; it’s very potent. We got our hands full. Defensively, they’re a lot like us. They don’t want you to run the ball on them. They’re going to make sure that they stop the run. They are disruptive, they’re long, they got versatility at the D line. There’s a wave of guys. They got two or three deep wave of guys that are good football players across the board that create havoc, and then here comes the pressure, here comes a lot of sticky man coverage, make you make accurate throws with people in your face, and make contested catches.”
